title: Urge surfing
hookLine: ride an urge like a wave until it passes, taught in relapse-prevention programs (Bowen and Marlatt)

lines: THE HAND REACHES FOR THE PHONE.
cards: Phone face down on the table. Ten seconds later, the hand is already reaching for it. Or the fridge door, opened for no reason.
Or the second drink, or the reply typed too fast. An urge arrives like a tug, and it seems to say: this will only get stronger until you give in.
The psychologist Alan Marlatt, who worked on helping people avoid relapse, offered a different picture: a wave in the ocean. Waves build, crest and break. Learning to ride one is today's word.

teach.b: Urge surfing treats a craving as a wave moving through the body. It rises, it peaks, and if you neither feed it nor fight it, it falls on its own. A surfer doesn't stop the wave, and doesn't let it knock them over.
They stay on top and ride it. Second, how it's done.

teach.h: THE URGE STAYED; THE SMOKING DROPPED.
teach.b: You turn toward the urge with curiosity. Where is it in the body? A tightness in the chest, an itch in the hands, a pull in the jaw?
Is it rising, holding steady, fading? The breath becomes the surfboard, something to stay balanced on while the wave goes by. Third, what a study found.
Sarah Bowen and Marlatt taught a brief version to college students who smoked. In the days that followed, the students taught to surf their urges smoked fewer cigarettes than a comparison group.
The urges themselves didn't get weaker. What changed was the step from urge to action. That's the honest center of the method: the wave still comes.

Fourth, an older root. Marlatt drew on Buddhist mindfulness practice. In the Buddha's teaching, a practitioner watches each feeling, pleasant, unpleasant or neither, as it arises and as it passes away.
The Pali word for craving is tanha, thirst.
It is treated as something to be seen clearly, not obeyed. An urge that is being watched has lost some of its hold on the hands.

how: In relapse-prevention programs, people are taught to notice where a craving sits in the body and to breathe with it as it rises and falls, before deciding whether to act.

o: pushing an urge down hard until it stops coming
riding a craving like a wave, not feeding or fighting it
giving in to an urge quickly so it passes sooner

games.q: mid-sit, an urge to check your phone shows up. what does urge surfing suggest?
o: grab it now, before the urge gets worse.
clench and force the thought away.
find where it sits in the body and breathe with it.
games.why: the method is neither feeding nor fighting: you watch the wave rise and fall, then decide.

practice: During the sit an urge may show up, to move, to scratch, to check the time, to stop; when it comes, don't act on it yet, and find where it lives in the body. Breathe with it and watch it rise, crest and fall.
If it's still there after a few breaths, you're free to act, slowly and on purpose; either way, you surfed.

wordCard.voice: Urge surfing. Riding a craving like a wave, watching it rise and fall in the body without feeding it or fighting it. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, from the Buddha's teaching: craving, literally 'thirst.'

carryVoice: Your line: surf it. The wave still comes, and it still breaks. That's today, done.
